_note: Pre-contact Mesoamerican routes: backstrap-loom cloth from cotton and maguey fibre, and charcoal-smelted silver without mercury. Alternatives to the Old World frame-loom textile chain and the amalgamation route, so a society holding only these nodes can supply cloth and silver (Complaints/closed/463).

maguey_fibre_kg.basis: per hectare of maguey (agave) managed for leaf fibre per year, as kg of cleaned dry fibre
maguey_fibre_kg.yield_basis: Yield: 500 kg of clean fibre per hectare a year sits inside the range PROSEA gives for sisal, the same genus (https://prosea.prota4u.org/view.aspx?id=6522, opened): 2.0 to 2.8 t/ha on the best plantations, about 1 t/ha on poorer soils, under 500 kg/ha in present Madura; leaf fibre content 3.5 to 4 percent. Scraping: the Mexican government lechuguilla fact sheet (https://www.gob.mx/cms/uploads/attachment/file/912100/Lechuguilla.pdf, opened) says one person scrapes 4 to 9 kg of fibre a working day, average 5 kg, from lechuguilla (fibre 8 to 12 percent of plant weight) with a blunt long knife against a wood block. Taken at the low end, 4 kg a day, for a stone or obsidian scraper and a maguey with less fibre per leaf than lechuguilla: 8 hours / 4 kg = 2 hours a kilogram, 1000 hours a hectare, replacing 8 hours a kilogram (4000 hours). The other 800 hours (planting offsets, weeding, cutting) have no source, so the row stays D; retire: Complaints/671 when a cultivation-labour source is read. The plant also yields sap, food and thorn needles; the whole hectare is charged to the fibre, which overstates fibre cost where those are co-products. PASS 9 (Complaint 671), opened: ojs.pphouse.org/index.php/IJBSM/article/download/116/93/167 (lechuguilla, Agave lecheguilla): manual shredders with a banco and an unsharpened knife extract 1.87 kg of dry fibre an hour, machines 15 to 18 kg, which is 0.53 hour per kilogram against the 8 hours used here (lechuguilla leaves are thin and the species wild, and the page gives no dry-fibre share of the leaf, so it is a floor on the hours, not a measurement of a maguey leaf scraped with stone); agritech.tnau.ac.in agave page: fibre content 2.5 to 4.5 percent (basis not stated), leaf yield 30 to 40 tonnes an acre from the third year, 40 to 50 leaves a plant a year, spacing 2 x 2 m (2,500 plants a hectare), which for a plantation sisal would be tonnes of fibre a hectare, above the 500 kg used for unmanaged Mexican maguey. ROUND 2, opened: Wikipedia, Henequen industry in Yucatan (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henequen_industry_in_Yucat%C3%A1n): holes 'about 8 feet (2.4 m) apart in each direction', 'Each plant yields 20 to 30 leaves yearly for a period of 12 to 20 years', 'It takes over 8,000 leaves to make a 400-pound bale'. Arithmetic: 10000 / (2.4 x 2.4) = 1736 plants a hectare; at 20 to 30 leaves, 35000 to 52000 leaves a hectare-year (43400 at 25); 400 lb = 181 kg over 8000 leaves = 22.7 kg of fibre per 1000 leaves, so 790 to 1180 kg a hectare, about 985 at 25 leaves. That is a machine-rasped plantation crop; 500 kg is half of it, inside 3x, and is kept for wild-grown, stone-scraped maguey. Cutting and weeding hours, from Alston, Mattiace and Nonnenmacher, Coercion, Culture and Debt Contracts: The Henequen Industry in Yucatan 1870-1915 (NBER w13852, https://nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w13852/w13852.pdf, opened and read with pdftotext): 'a typical worker weeded 1-2 mecates or cut roughly 2000 leaves' a day, 'Roughly 25 mecates are in a hectare', and Hartman's 'three thousand leaves, an effort that could be performed without strain in six to eight hours'. Cutting: 43400 leaves / 2000 a day = 22 days, at 8 hours 174 hours. Weeding: 25 mecates / 1.5 a day = 17 days = 133 hours a pass, two passes a year assumed (assumption, no source for the frequency) = 267 hours. Planting offsets: 1736 plants replaced over a 15-year life is 116 a year, at an assumed 0.1 hour each, 12 hours (assumption). Scraping: 1000 hours (above, lechuguilla fact sheet). Total 174 + 267 + 12 + 1000 = 1453 hours; 1800 is within 3x and is kept. Cutting at 2000 leaves a day assumes the labourer cuts and trims only; the Mexican hand rate is from haciendas, a modern-era labour norm used as an analogue. Every figure is sourced, derived or a labelled assumption.

fabric_backstrap_cotton_kg.basis: per kg of plain cotton fabric woven on the backstrap loom, off the loom and unfinished
fabric_backstrap_cotton_kg.yield_basis: LABELLED HEURISTIC (conf D). Fibre loss 10 percent in cleaning, carding by hand and spinning (the same allowance as cotton_fabric_kg). Spinning fine cotton on a supported spindle with a whorl is the slowest step: taken at 25 grams of thread per hour, 40 hours per kilogram. A backstrap loom is warped, then woven a hand's breadth of shed at a time with a batten and a stick shuttle, the weaver sitting or kneeling and leaning on the strap to keep the warp taut; narrow cloth of a body's width in plain weave, taken at 20 grams of cloth per hour including warping and setting up, 50 hours per kilogram. The ethnographic backstrap weaving record gives a plain woven cloth the size of a shawl or blouse panel in days; the grams-per-hour figures here are chosen to match that order and are not read from a source. The loom itself is sticks, a strap and a batten, so no capital is charged. Sources: Berdan, The Aztecs of Central Mexico (1982), on cotton and maguey cloth and the tribute in cloth; Brumfiel on Aztec cloth tribute and household spinning and weaving; Sahagun, Florentine Codex books 9 and 10, on the metalworkers' blowpipe and charcoal furnaces; Hosler, The Sounds and Colors of Power (1994), on pre-contact Mesoamerican metallurgy. None was read for a number here: quantities are labelled heuristics, conf D, and are the first thing to replace with a measured figure. PASS 9 (Complaint 671), opened: gansey.blogspot.com 2021/06 how-fast-can-hand-spinner-spin: a wheel makes worsted singles of 11,200 yards a pound at about 400 yards an hour (0.0357 lb, 16 g an hour, 62 hours a kilogram), 24,000 yards a pound at 350 yards an hour, and a half ounce of 11,200 yards a pound took about 90 minutes; spinoffmagazine.com productive-spindle-spinning: a supported spindle (takli) can run at 3 yards a minute on fine yarn; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weaving: a very good handloom weaver wove two pieces of 24 yards of shirting a week (a treadle handloom, not a backstrap). The 25 g an hour of spinning (40 hours a kilogram) is faster than the wheel figure at a medium count and the thread count of Mexican cloth is not in any opened page, so the spinner and weaver hours are not bounded. No Mexicolore, Smith and Hirth or Nichols page with times could be opened. ROUND 2, opened: Hand Woven magazine, Improving lives one handwoven bag at a time (https://handwovenmagazine.com/improving-lives-one-handwoven-bag-at-a-time/): backstrap weavers 'generally work for 6 to 8 hours a week' 'producing about 100 inches of cloth in that time', on '15 inch backstrap looms with 330-end commercially dyed cotton warps' (a modern workshop, used as the analogue). Weaving rate: 100 in x 15 in = 1500 sq in = 0.968 sq m in 7 hours, 0.138 sq m an hour, 7.2 hours a square metre. Cloth mass, with the yarn count an ASSUMPTION (no Mesoamerican count read): 330 ends over 15 in is 22 a inch, an assumed equal 22 picks a inch gives 44 threads an inch, 1732 a metre of cloth; cotton of English count 10 (10 x 840 yd a lb, 16.9 m a gram, 0.059 g a metre) makes 1732 x 0.059 = 102 g a sq m, and count 20 half of that. Weaver hours a kilogram at count 10: 7.2 / 0.102 = 71; at count 20: 141; the 50 used here is inside 3x of both. Spinning: Spin Off, Productive spindle spinning: yes you can (https://spinoffmagazine.com/productive-spindle-spinning-yes-you-can/, opened) gives 'three yards per minute or better' on a takli for garment-weight singles, 180 yd an hour; at count 10 (8400 yd a lb) that is 9.7 g an hour, 103 hours a kilogram; at count 5, 52 hours a kilogram; with the opened wheel figure above (16 g an hour) the 40 here is inside 3x. Huipil weight: Mayan Boutique ceremonial cotton huipil listing (https://www.mayanboutique.com/en/huipils/439-huipil-ceremonial.html, opened): shipping weight 1000 g, 'six months for its elaboration' (a brocaded ceremonial piece, a heavy upper case, not used). All numbers are now sourced, derived or a labelled assumption (the yarn count).

fabric_backstrap_maguey_kg.basis: per kg of coarse maguey-fibre fabric woven on the backstrap loom, off the loom and unfinished
fabric_backstrap_maguey_kg.yield_basis: LABELLED HEURISTIC (conf D). Maguey (ixtle) fibre is long and coarse, so it twists to a thicker thread than cotton and a given mass of thread is shorter: fewer hours per kilogram to spin and weave than cotton, 50 and 40. Fibre loss 15 percent in combing out the short pieces and in twisting, as for coarse bast fibres in canvas_kg. Maguey cloth was the commoner's cloth, rougher and cheaper than cotton, which the nobility wore (Berdan). The loom is the same backstrap loom. Sources: Berdan, The Aztecs of Central Mexico (1982), on cotton and maguey cloth and the tribute in cloth; Brumfiel on Aztec cloth tribute and household spinning and weaving; Sahagun, Florentine Codex books 9 and 10, on the metalworkers' blowpipe and charcoal furnaces; Hosler, The Sounds and Colors of Power (1994), on pre-contact Mesoamerican metallurgy. None was read for a number here: quantities are labelled heuristics, conf D, and are the first thing to replace with a measured figure. PASS 9: see fabric_backstrap_cotton_kg; the lechuguilla paper gives no spinning or weaving rate for ixtle thread. Stays D. Round 4 (Pass 14) bracket, by the cotton row's own method. Yarn weight: UNIDO, The Processing and Use of Indigenous Fibres, final report (Oxenham and Smith; https://downloads.unido.org/ot/48/40/4840894/15001-20000_18458.pdf, opened with pdftotext): 100 percent maguey after carding and gilling 'could be spin to 200tex' (a laboratory machine-spun yarn, a modern analogue for coarse hand thread), against the cotton row's assumed count 10 of 59 tex (0.059 g a metre), 3.4 times as heavy a metre. If a metre of thread cost the same time to spin and weave whatever its weight, hours a kilogram fall by 3.4, to 12 spinner and 15 weaver hours; if coarse tough fibre is as slow per kilogram as cotton, they stay 40 and 50 (the cotton row). The value is set between the two ends: spinner 20 (was 50), weaver 25 (was 40). tried: Berdan and Brumfiel (not opened), a search for ayate cloth weight (none), UNIDO (used).

cloth_backstrap_kg.basis: per kg of finished cloth from backstrap-woven fabric
cloth_backstrap_kg.yield_basis: LABELLED HEURISTIC (conf D). Finishing here is washing out the sizing and dirt, beating the cloth with a smooth stone or mallet to close the weave, and drying; no fulling mill or tenter frame. The same 5 percent loss as cloth_kg. Gated on the backstrap loom because the only fabric the Mexica can make is backstrap fabric; cloth_kg's own entry needs fulling. Sources: Berdan, The Aztecs of Central Mexico (1982), on cotton and maguey cloth and the tribute in cloth; Brumfiel on Aztec cloth tribute and household spinning and weaving; Sahagun, Florentine Codex books 9 and 10, on the metalworkers' blowpipe and charcoal furnaces; Hosler, The Sounds and Colors of Power (1994), on pre-contact Mesoamerican metallurgy. None was read for a number here: quantities are labelled heuristics, conf D, and are the first thing to replace with a measured figure. PASS 9: no opened page gives a beating and washing time for handwoven cloth. Stays D. Round 4 (Pass 14) tried: comparable (the fuller hours of cloth_kg in 40_organics, a fulling-mill row, do not fit a stone-beaten cloth), rate (a time-use or laundry-by-beating rate: Rachel Laudan and Spin Off pages opened earlier give spinning and grinding only), stand-in (none found for washing and beating a handwoven cloth). Missing: minutes per kilogram of cloth to wash, beat and dry by hand.

silver_smelted_native_kg.basis: per tonne of silver won by direct charcoal smelting of silver ore (native silver and silver sulphides) in small blowpipe-fired furnaces, no mercury and no lead collector
silver_smelted_native_kg.yield_basis: LABELLED HEURISTIC (conf D) for the quantities; the technique is attested. Pre-contact Mesoamerican and Andean metalworkers smelted and melted silver in small charcoal furnaces blown through blowpipes or by many mouths, and hammered, cast (lost wax) and soldered it (Sahagun, Florentine Codex book 9; Hosler 1994 for West Mexico), with no mercury, which arrived with the colonial patio process. Ore grade is the silver_kg entry's (the silver-only deposits of data/world/geography/deposits/ancient.json), so ore per kilogram is that entry's figure scaled from its 75 percent recovery to 80 percent for a direct smelt of native silver and rich oxidised ore that needs no amalgamation. Dressing is the same 85 labourer hours per tonne of rock as silver_kg and the lead route (sim/world/ore_dressing.py). Charcoal 0.3 kg per kg of dressed ore and furnaceman hours 0.113 per kg of ore are the silver_jarosite_kg per-kg-of-ore figures rounded, minus its lead collector and cupellation. No source gives a Mexica furnace's fuel or hours. Sources: Berdan, The Aztecs of Central Mexico (1982), on cotton and maguey cloth and the tribute in cloth; Brumfiel on Aztec cloth tribute and household spinning and weaving; Sahagun, Florentine Codex books 9 and 10, on the metalworkers' blowpipe and charcoal furnaces; Hosler, The Sounds and Colors of Power (1994), on pre-contact Mesoamerican metallurgy. None was read for a number here: quantities are labelled heuristics, conf D, and are the first thing to replace with a measured figure. PASS 9: no opened page gives a Mesoamerican furnace fuel or hours; the 80 percent recovery has the same missing input as silver_jarosite_kg. Stays D. Round 4 (Pass 14) stand-in, REPORTED NOT APPLIED: the best documented Andean practice, a huayrachina wind furnace worked by Carlos Cuiza near Porco, Bolivia. Cohen, Van Buren, Mills and others, 'Current silver smelting in the Bolivian Andes: a review of the technology employed', Historical Metallurgy 44(2), 2010 (https://www.hmsjournal.org/index.php/home/article/download/155/151, opened with pdftotext, Table 1): charges of about 20 kg (galena with recycled reacted cupellation hearth material at 2:1) burned about 10 kg of charcoal, 'a fuel-to-charge ratio of around 1:2', and 'The smelting process lasted up to eight hours'. That is 0.5 kg of charcoal (held 0.3, within 3x, agrees) and 8 / 20 = 0.4 furnace hours per kilogram of charge (held 0.113, 3.5x lower, outside the 3x rule). Applying 0.5 and 0.4 (841,875 kg and 673,500 hours a tonne), or the charcoal alone, raised the spread of the starting-wage metal cost between civilisations above the 1.25 that sim/tests/test_opening_wage_anchor.py holds (1.2566 and 1.2755), so the values are left as they were and the decision is the orchestrator's. This is also a lead-silver smelt, a stand-in for a direct silver smelt that may take less. Conf stays D. tried: Hosler and Sahagun (not opened), Cohen et al. (used), the wage-anchor test.
